definition: A scientific investigation is a systematic scientific method used by scientists or researchers to solve problems related to science.
key_principle: A scientific investigation must follow a specific sequence of steps starting from an initial observation of a phenomenon to conducting a controlled experiment where variables are manipulated, allowing the researcher to make data-driven conclusions about a hypothesis.

essential_data.title: Steps in a Scientific Method
items: 1. Making observations: Using senses to gather information about an object or phenomenon.
2. Making an inference: Using data collection and past experience to make a conclusion and explanation.
3. Identifying the problem: Asking questions based on the inference made.
4. Making a hypothesis: Making a general, testable statement about the relationship between a manipulated variable and a responding variable.
5. Identifying the variables: Identifying manipulated, responding, and fixed variables.
6. Controlling the variables: Manipulating one variable while keeping others fixed to observe relationships.
7. Planning an experiment: Determining materials, apparatus, procedure, and data analysis methods.
8. Collecting data: Making observations or measurements and recording them systematically.
9. Interpreting data: Organising and analyzing data through calculations, graphs, or charts.
10. Making a conclusion: Stating whether the hypothesis is accepted or rejected based on results.
11. Preparing a report: Communicating details of the experiment to share findings.

topic_title: Usage, Management and Handling of Apparatus and Materials
definition: This section outlines the essential safety measures, personal protective equipment (PPE), and standard operating procedures for managing, storing, and disposing of laboratory chemicals to prevent accidents and environmental pollution.
key_principle: Chemicals pose different risks (e.g., toxicity, flammability, corrosiveness) and must be rigorously sorted, securely stored, handled using proper protective equipment, and disposed of according to standard environmental procedures to avoid hazards like mercury poisoning or explosive reactions.

essential_data.title: Personal Protective Equipment and Safety Equipment
rows: Prevents dust or splashes of chemicals from getting into the eyes.
Protects the body and clothing against chemical spills such as acids, alkalis, and organic solvents.
Protects hands from injuries, chemicals, or infections when handling substances.
Protects respiratory organs from chemicals in the form of powder or fumes.
Protects the feet from injuries caused by chemical spills, sharp objects, or toxic substances.
Specially designed equipment for experiments that release toxic vapours, cause combustions, or produce pungent smells.
Washes and cleans the body in the event of a chemical accident; also extinguishes fire on clothing.
Washes and cleans the eye when accidents occur to parts of the eye.

essential_data.title: Storage of Chemicals
items: Reactive substances (e.g., Lithium, Sodium, Potassium): Stored in paraffin oil to prevent reaction with moisture in the air.
Hydrocarbons and organic solvents: Stored in shady areas far from sunlight and heat sources due to volatility and flammability.
Substances that decompose easily (e.g., Nitric acid, Hydrogen peroxide, Liquid bromine): Stored in dark bottles to prevent decomposition from light exposure.
Corrosive substances (pH<5 and pH>9): Stored in special, locked storage cabinets.
Heavy metals and toxic substances: Kept in special labelled containers in a locked, heat-free room.

essential_data.title: Disposal of Chemicals
items: Hydrogen peroxide: Low concentration can be poured down the sink; high concentration must be diluted with water and added to sodium sulphite before disposal.
Solid wastes (e.g., glass, rubber): Disposed of into special containers.
Organic solvents and hydrocarbons: Kept in special glass or plastic containers (cannot be poured in the sink as they pollute the water source).
Strong acids and alkalis: Kept in closed, labelled containers.
Heavy metals and toxic substances: Solutions kept in plastic bags, evaporated in a fume chamber, tied carefully, and placed in heavy metal waste containers.
Volatile substances: Stored in closed containers away from sun and heat.

essential_data.title: Emergency Management Procedure for Spills
items: Inform your teacher or the laboratory assistant about the accident immediately.
Prohibit other students from entering the accident site.
Stop the spill from spreading to other areas by using sand to border it.
Clean the chemical spill.
Dispose of the chemical spill by following the correct procedures.

definition: Matter is something that has mass and occupies space, and it consists of tiny, discrete particles. Matter can exist in three states: solid, liquid, and gas.

topic_title: The Development of the Atomic Model
definition: An atom is the basic building block of matter, composed of three subatomic particles: protons, neutrons, and electrons.
key_principle: The atomic structure model was developed over time by various scientists, culminating in the modern understanding that an atom consists of a dense nucleus (containing positively charged protons and neutral neutrons) surrounded by negatively charged electrons moving in shells.

essential_data.title: Historical Development of the Atomic Model
items: John Dalton (1766 – 1844): Proposed that matter is made of indestructible, indivisible spherical atoms. Elements of the same type have the same atoms.
J.J. Thomson (1856 – 1940): Discovered electrons and proposed a positively-charged sphere with negatively-charged electrons embedded in it.
Ernest Rutherford (1871 – 1937): Discovered the nucleus containing positively-charged protons, where almost all atomic mass is concentrated, with electrons moving outside it.
Niels Bohr (1885 – 1962): Proposed that electrons move in fixed shells around the nucleus.
James Chadwick (1891 – 1974): Discovered neutral particles called neutrons in the nucleus, which contribute to almost half of the atom's mass.

chapter_title: Chapter 3: The Mole Concept, Chemical Formula and Equation
topic_title: Relative Atomic Mass and Relative Molecular Mass
definition: Relative atomic mass (RAM) is the average mass of an atom of an element compared to $\frac{1}{12}$ of the mass of one carbon-12 atom. Similarly, relative molecular mass (RMM) is the average mass of a molecule compared to $\frac{1}{12}$ of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.
key_principle: Atoms and molecules are too small to be weighed directly, so chemists compare their masses to a standard atom (carbon-12). For compounds, the relative molecular mass (for molecules) or relative formula mass (for ionic substances) is calculated by summing up the relative atomic masses of all the atoms present in the formula.
formula: $\text{Relative atomic mass of an element} = \frac{\text{Average mass of one atom of the element}}{\frac{1}{12} \times \text{Mass of one carbon-12 atom}}$ $\text{Relative molecular mass of a substance} = \frac{\text{Average mass of one molecule}}{\frac{1}{12} \times \text{Mass of one carbon-12 atom}}$

essential_data.title: Examples of Calculating Relative Mass
items: RMM of oxygen gas, O₂: $2 \times (\text{RAM of O}) = 2(16) = 32$
RMM of water, H₂O: $2 \times (\text{RAM of H}) + \text{RAM of O} = 2(1) + 16 = 18$
RFM of zinc chloride, ZnCl₂: $\text{RAM of Zn} + 2 \times (\text{RAM of Cl}) = 65 + 2(35.5) = 136$

chapter_title: Chapter 3: The Mole Concept, Chemical Formula and Equation
definition: The mole is the SI unit used to measure the amount of substance in chemistry. One mole of a substance contains $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ particles, a value known as the Avogadro constant.
key_principle: The mole acts as a central conversion factor in chemistry. The number of moles can be used to interconnect the number of particles (using the Avogadro constant), the mass of a substance (using molar mass), and the volume of a gas (using molar volume).
formula: $n = \frac{\text{Number of particles}}{N_A}$ $n = \frac{\text{Mass (g)}}{\text{Molar mass (g mol}^{-1}\text{)}}$ $n = \frac{\text{Volume of gas}}{\text{Molar volume}}$
variables: n: Number of moles N_A: Avogadro constant ($6.02 \times 10^{23} \text{ mol}^{-1}$) Mass: The mass of the substance in grams (g) Molar mass: The mass of one mole of the substance in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$ (equivalent in value to RAM/RMM/RFM) Volume of gas: The space occupied by the gas in $\text{dm}^3$ or $\text{cm}^3$ Molar volume: Volume of 1 mole of gas ($\text{22.4 dm}^3 \text{ mol}^{-1}$ at STP or $\text{24 dm}^3 \text{ mol}^{-1}$ at room conditions)

definition: A chemical formula is a representation of a chemical substance using alphabets to represent the atoms and subscript numbers to show the number of each type of atom found in the basic entities of the substance.

definition: A chemical equation is a shorthand description of a chemical reaction using chemical formulae, showing the reactants on the left-hand side and the products on the right-hand side.
key_principle: Based on the law of conservation of mass, a chemical equation must be balanced so that the number of atoms of each element is equal on both sides. Balanced chemical equations allow for stoichiometry—the quantitative study of the exact composition and mole ratio of substances involved in a reaction.

definition: The Periodic Table of Elements is a system that classifies known chemical elements in a table according to certain characteristics, developed through the contributions of multiple scientists over time.
key_principle: The fundamental principle of the modern Periodic Table is that elements are arranged in ascending order of their proton numbers (from 1 to 118), and elements with similar chemical properties are placed in the same vertical columns.

essential_data.title: Historical Development of the Periodic Table of Elements
items: Antoine Lavoisier (1743 – 1794): Classified elements into four groups (gases, non-metals, metals, and metal oxides), though inaccurate because he included light and heat.
Johann W. Dobereiner (1780 – 1849): Classified elements with similar chemical properties into groups of three called triads, noting the relationship between atomic mass and chemical properties.
John Newlands (1837 – 1898): Arranged elements by increasing atomic mass and proposed the Law of Octaves, as properties recurred every eighth element.
Lothar Meyer (1830 – 1895): Plotted atomic volume against atomic mass and found elements at equivalent positions on the curve had similar chemical properties.

Dmitri Mendeleev (1834 – 1907): Arranged elements by increasing atomic mass and placed elements with similar properties in the same vertical columns, leaving empty spaces to successfully predict undiscovered elements.
Henry Moseley (1887 – 1915): Discovered the relationship between X-ray spectrums and proton numbers, leading to the modern arrangement of elements by increasing proton numbers.

definition: Neutralisation is a chemical reaction between an acid and an alkali (base) to produce salt and water only, where the acid loses its acidity and the alkali loses its alkalinity.
key_principle: The actual reaction only involves the combination of hydrogen ions ($H^+$) from the acid and hydroxide ions ($OH^-$) from the alkali to produce neutral water molecules. The end point of titration is determined when an acid-base indicator changes colour.
formula: Ionic equation: $H^+(aq) + OH^-(aq) \rightarrow H_2O(l)$. Calculation formula: $\frac{M_aV_a}{M_bV_b} = \frac{a}{b}$.
variables: $M_a, M_b$: Molarity of acid A and alkali B. $V_a, V_b$: Volume of acid A and alkali B. $a, b$: Mole ratio from the balanced chemical equation representing acid A and alkali B.

definition: A salt is an ionic compound formed when the hydrogen ion ($H^+$) from an acid is replaced with a metal ion or an ammonium ion ($NH_4^+$).
key_principle: All salts form crystals that possess highly specific geometrical shapes due to the orderly and compact arrangement of particles in their solid lattice structures.

definition: The rate of reaction is the measurement of the change in the quantity of reactants or products per unit of time, which can be observed and measured.
key_principle: Chemical reactions can be classified as either fast (e.g., explosions) or slow (e.g., rusting). The rate of reaction can be measured as the average rate of reaction (the average value over a specific time interval) or the instantaneous rate of reaction (the rate at a specific point of time, determined by calculating the gradient of the tangent to the curve on a graph).
formula: Average rate of reaction = $\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta t} = \frac{V_2 - V_1}{t_2 - t_1}$ Instantaneous rate of reaction at time $t$ = Gradient of the tangent at time $t$
variables: $V_1, V_2$: Volume of gas collected (or quantity of substance) at specific times. $t_1, t_2$: Specific time points. $\Delta V$: Change in the quantity of reactants or products. $\Delta t$: Time taken for the change to occur.

Changes in pressure: Measured using a pressure meter for gas reactions.
Changes in electrical conductivity: Measured using an ammeter for mobile ions.
Changes in pH values: Measured using a pH meter.

essential_data.title: Classification of Rate of Reactions
items: Fast Reactions: Electric cells reaction, ignition of matches, combustion of gases, fireworks.

definition: Different chemical substances have different chemical properties and react at different rates depending on four main physical factors: size of reactants, concentration, temperature, and presence of a catalyst.
key_principle: The rate of reaction increases when the size of solid reactants decreases (which increases the total exposed surface area), the concentration of aqueous reactants increases, the temperature of the reaction increases, or when a suitable positive catalyst is added. For gaseous reactions, an increase in gas pressure acts similarly to concentration by pushing particles into a smaller volume.

essential_data.title: Factors Affecting Rate of Reaction
items: Size of Reactants: Smaller pieces of solid reactants possess a larger total surface area compared to a single large piece of the same mass, leading to a higher rate of reaction.
Concentration: Adding more solute to a fixed volume of solvent increases concentration, leading to a higher rate of reaction.
Temperature: Increasing the heat of a reaction increases the rate of reaction.
Presence of a Catalyst: A catalyst alters the rate of reaction but remains chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction (the mass of the catalyst does not change before and after the reaction).
Pressure (for gases): Compressing a gas at a constant temperature increases its concentration, thus increasing the rate of reaction.

topic_title: Application of Factors that Affect the Rate of Reaction in Daily Life
definition: The manipulation of factors that affect the rate of reaction—such as size, temperature, concentration, and catalysts—is widely applied in domestic chores, medicine, and industrial processes to control how fast or slow a reaction occurs.
key_principle: We increase the rate of reaction to make processes faster and more efficient (like cutting potatoes into strips to cook them faster or using a catalytic converter in cars), and we decrease the rate of reaction to delay unwanted processes (like keeping food in a refrigerator to slow down bacterial decay).

essential_data.title: Real-World Applications of Reaction Rates
items: Size Factor: Chewing antacid tablets (breaking them into smaller pieces) increases the surface area, speeding up the neutralisation of stomach acid. Cutting potatoes into thin strips cooks them faster.

Temperature Factor: Storing food in a refrigerator lowers the temperature, slowing down the rate of food decay. Frying food in oil (which can reach 180°C) cooks food much faster than boiling in water (100°C).

Concentration Factor: Compressing petrol vapour and air in a car engine increases its concentration so it burns and explodes rapidly to power the car. High concentrations of acidic pollutants in industrial areas increase the rate of corrosion of iron buildings.

Catalyst Factor: Catalytic converters in cars use a platinum ($Pt$) catalyst to quickly convert harmful exhaust pollutants (unburned hydrocarbons, $CO$, $NO_x$) into safer gases ($H_2O$, $CO_2$, $N_2$). Yeast acts as a biological catalyst in the fermentation of glucose to produce ethanol.

definition: The collision theory explains that for a chemical reaction to occur, reactant particles must constantly move and collide with one another with sufficient energy and in the correct orientation to break old bonds and form new ones.
key_principle: The rate of reaction depends directly on the frequency of effective collisions. An effective collision only occurs if particles collide with a minimum threshold energy called the activation energy ($E_a$) and in the proper orientation. Altering factors like temperature, concentration, surface area, or adding a catalyst directly influences the frequency of these effective collisions.
variables: $E_a$: Activation energy (the energy barrier required to start a reaction). $E_a'$: Activation energy with a catalyst (which is lower than $E_a$). $\Delta H$: Heat of reaction (the change in energy content between reactants and products).

essential_data.title: How Factors Influence the Collision Theory
items: Concentration/Pressure: Increases the number of particles per unit volume $\rightarrow$ frequency of collisions between particles increases $\rightarrow$ frequency of effective collisions increases $\rightarrow$ rate of reaction increases.

Size of Reactant: Increases total surface area exposed to collision $\rightarrow$ frequency of collisions between particles increases $\rightarrow$ frequency of effective collisions increases $\rightarrow$ rate of reaction increases.

Temperature: Increases the kinetic energy of particles $\rightarrow$ more particles possess energy $\ge E_a$ $\rightarrow$ frequency of effective collisions increases $\rightarrow$ rate of reaction increases.

Presence of Catalyst: Provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy ($E_a'$) $\rightarrow$ more reactant particles can achieve the new activation energy $\rightarrow$ frequency of effective collisions increases $\rightarrow$ rate of reaction increases.

essential_data.title: Energy Profile Diagrams
rows: Total energy of reactants is higher than products. $\Delta H$ is negative (heat released to surroundings).
Total energy of products is higher than reactants. $\Delta H$ is positive (heat absorbed from surroundings).

definition: An alloy is a mixture of two or more elements where the main element is a metal.
key_principle: The alloying process is used to prevent the corrosion of metal and to alter the properties of a pure metal to make it harder and stronger. In a pure metal, atoms are of the same size and arranged in an orderly manner, allowing layers to easily slide over each other when force is applied (making them ductile and malleable). In an alloy, foreign atoms of different sizes disrupt this orderly arrangement, preventing the layers of atoms from sliding easily, which results in a stronger and harder material.

essential_data.title: Examples of Alloys and Their Uses
items: Pewter: Used to make souvenirs.
Duralumin: Used to make the body of an aeroplane.
Bronze: Used to make medals and monuments.
Brass: Used to make keys.
Steel: Used to make the body of a car.
Stainless steel: Used to make cutlery due to its resistance to corrosion.
Superconductor: Used to make magnets that can levitate Maglev trains and move them at high speeds without electrical resistance at very low temperatures.

topic_title: Composition of Glass and Its Uses
definition: Glass is a non-metallic material produced when silica (silicon dioxide, SiO₂) is heated together with other chemicals.
key_principle: Various types of glass with different properties can be obtained by altering the chemicals heated alongside silica, though all types of glass share the same fundamental physical properties such as being hard but brittle, and acting as heat and electrical insulators.

essential_data.title: Basic Properties of Glass
items: Hard but brittle
Electrical insulator
Heat insulator
Waterproof
Chemically inert
Transparent

essential_data.title: Types of Glass
items: Fused silica glass: Made purely from silica.
Soda-lime glass: Made from silica (SiO₂), soda (sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃), and limestone (calcium carbonate, CaCO₃).
Borosilicate glass: Made of silica, boron oxide (B₂O₃), and alumina (Al₂O₃).
Lead crystal glass: Contains lead components.

topic_title: Composition of Ceramics and Its Uses
definition: A ceramic is a solid made up of inorganic and non-metallic substances (such as metal compounds, non-metal compounds, or metalloid compounds) that is produced through a process of shaping and hardening by using heating techniques at a very high temperature.
key_principle: The atoms in ceramics are bonded by strong covalent bonds and ionic bonds, causing them to melt only at very high temperatures and making them hard and resistant to compression. However, because the atoms are strongly bonded in a rigid arrangement, they cannot slide over each other; force applied breaks the bonds instead, making ceramics brittle and weak towards stretching.

essential_data.title: Basic Properties of Ceramics
items: High thermal resistant
Hard and strong (resistant to compression)
Break easily (brittle)
Chemically inert
Heat and electrical insulator (electrons cannot move freely)

essential_data.title: Ceramic Uses and Applications
rows: Zirconia ceramic is used in dental implants. Alumina ceramic is used to make knee bones. Ceramics with superconductivity are used in MRI machines.
Engine components in jet planes are made from ceramics.
Used to make electrical insulators in high voltage areas such as power stations.

definition: A composite material is a structural material made by combining two or more non-homogeneous substances, specifically a matrix substance and a strengthening substance.
key_principle: In a composite, the matrix substance surrounds and binds the strengthening substance together. The resulting composite material generally exhibits superior or completely different physical properties compared to its original, individual components.

essential_data.title: Comparison of Composite Materials and Their Original Components
rows: Concrete withstands compression but breaks under stretching; combining it with steel increases its ability to withstand stretching forces. Used in bridges and dams.
Weak, soft, and easily burned plastic is reinforced to become strong while maintaining low heat and electrical conductivity.
Achieves high compression strength despite the original glass being brittle; used to transmit information and data.
Normal glass is transparent but doesn't absorb UV. The composite remains transparent to visible light but darkens to absorb UV rays.
Conducts electrical current without any resistance at very low temperatures, unlike its original components.
